title: Why Behavior Has Gotten Worse And What To Do About It o-do-about-it/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Citing a National Center for Education Statistics finding that 56 percent of school leaders report increased misbehavior since the pandemic, Linsin argues the pandemic itself isn't the real cause — the continued rise in misbehavior nearly two years into in-person learning points instead to school leaders lowering standards on dress codes, discipline policies, phone use, and consequences in an effort to appear understanding. He describes serious offenses like assault or threats resulting in students being back in class hours later with no real consequence, forcing teachers to lower their own standards just to survive. His two-part solution is for staff to unite, build or rebuild a precise school-wide discipline plan with specific in-class and administrative consequences and alternatives to suspension, and present it to administration; and, failing that, for individual teachers to bring discipline to their own classrooms through expert classroom management and the mental toughness to sustain it.
points: 56 percent of school leaders report increased misbehavior since the pandemic, per an NCES survey Linsin cites.
He argues the real cause isn't the pandemic itself but school leaders lowering standards on dress code, phone use, and discipline.
Serious offenses like assault or threats often result in students returning to class within hours with no real consequence.
His first recommended solution is a united staff building a precise, school-wide discipline plan with specific consequences and alternatives to suspension.
His fallback solution for individual teachers is bringing expert classroom management and mental toughness to their own classroom regardless of school-wide dysfunction.
quotes: According to a National Center for Education Statistics survey, 56 percent of school leaders believe the pandemic has led to an increase of student misbehavior.

In an effort to be “understanding,” they lowered standards. They loosened dress codes, ignored discipline policies, capitulated on phone use, allowed abhorrent language in the hallways, and removed consequences.
Thus, if a teacher gets threatened or a student gets assaulted, and the teacher reports the offense—which they must do—the perpetrator is right back in the classroom hours later.
You must gather as a staff and speak up. You must decide as teachers that enough is enough and you’re going to have each other’s backs.
You just need two things: Expert classroom management. Mental toughness.
Bottom line is that what has happened since the pandemic is wrong, every which way. It’s tragic.
